meta.regime: The energy shock has stopped being a one-way dollar trade and become a global tightening impulse, and that is the single most important change on this board today. For a week the framing was that crude up 10% forced the Fed's hand and everything else was collateral; this afternoon the Bank of Canada and the Bank of Japan both told the market the same shock is forcing THEIR hands too - Macklem explicitly raising the possibility of more than one hike, Ueda explicitly naming upside price risks before a live September meeting - while the US data missed for a third consecutive session. The result is that the dollar is now the currency with the weakest incremental case among the tighteners, not the strongest, and the board has four currencies at +1 or better against a soft, mixed dollar. Underneath it the Strait itself is genuinely two-sided: two supertankers were hit by projectiles on Monday night and the US struck southern Iran again overnight, but the US Energy Secretary says over 17 million barrels a day transited on Tuesday, the highest since the conflict began. The risk premium is in the price; the physical disruption, so far, is not.

dailyRead: This is an afternoon rewrite of the morning file, and it is warranted because two central banks changed the board after it was published. Start with Canada, because it is the day's cleanest reversal. The Bank of Canada held the overnight rate at 2.25% for a seventh straight meeting, with the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%, exactly as all 35 economists polled expected and with no Monetary Policy Report. The morning file said the statement language was the entire event and warned that heavy tariff-risk wording would take CAD back to zero. The statement went the other way. It says the conflict in the Middle East is keeping energy prices higher for longer and that this has INCREASED the upside risks to the outlook for inflation, that there has been little progress reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and that the longer high oil prices and elevated refinery margins persist the greater the risk of spillover into the prices of other goods and services. It also says economic growth has picked up after stalling for the past year, putting Canada on a stronger footing. Macklem then removed any ambiguity in the press conference: if inflation is going to remain too high, the Bank is prepared to raise rates, and in his own words, if it takes more than one increase, they are prepared to do that. Note the honesty of the inflation composition he was working from - headline is 3.0% on gasoline, but ex-gasoline it is 2.2% and the core measures were close to 2% in July - which means this is a central bank pre-committing to defend against a shock it has not yet seen in its underlying data. That is hawkish, and the tape agreed: USD/CAD fell to 1.38455, down 0.36% on the day and 1.44% on the month, with the loonie finally being paid for WTI at 90.903 and up 10.60% on the week. CAD is upgraded from +1 to +2. Japan is the second upgrade and it is the more consequential one for this book. Governor Ueda said the Bank will consider a rate hike at every policy meeting including the September 17-18 meeting, and that he will decide policy with upside price risks in mind - naming the Middle East conflict, robust AI-related demand and the inflation boost from a weak yen as the specific factors under scrutiny. He also addressed the bond market directly, framing the rise in the 10-year JGB to around 3.00%, the first time since 1996, as largely a global phenomenon rather than a domestic policy signal, while saying the Bank will stay vigilant. That is a Governor doing exactly what the morning file said would repair the yen leg, and he did it hours after Takata - the lone July dissenter for 1.25% - renewed his push for consecutive hikes in Sapporo. The market responded: USD/JPY broke down 0.84% to 158.839, off the 160 line both capitals had defended since the July 31 joint intervention, and the Nikkei fell 2.60% to 64,495 with SoftBank down 6.4% and Tokyo Electron down 3.4%, which is the equity market pricing the same thing. JPY is upgraded from 0 to +1. The honest caveat is that the energy shock remains a straight terms-of-trade hit on Japan - the trade balance is minus 634 billion yen and the current account swung to minus 923 billion - so this is a policy-expectations upgrade, not an economic one. The third change is the dollar, and it is a downgrade. ADP private payrolls rose just 38,000 in August against a 47,000 consensus and a revised 46,000 in July, the weakest month since January, with manufacturing shedding 17,000 and professional and business services 16,000 while education and health carried the entire number at plus 45,000; base pay growth is 3.2%. That is the third consecutive US data miss after ISM manufacturing at 54.6 and JOLTS at 7.271 million. Factory orders did beat at plus 0.9% against plus 0.6%, so the picture is not uniform, but the direction of surprise is clear and the tape now agrees: DXY is 99.566 and down 0.11%, and the dollar lost ground to both of today's upgrades. The morning file held USD at +1 on the argument that the market had stopped trading US activity and started trading the energy-inflation channel. That argument was correct at the time and it is precisely what broke this afternoon, because the same energy channel is now driving BoC and BoJ expectations too - so it is no longer a dollar-differentiating story. FedWatch is still around 66% for September 16 and payrolls on Friday at plus 58,000 consensus is the resolving event, but until it prints the dollar has no incremental case over Canada, the euro area, Australia or Japan. USD is downgraded from +1 to 0. The geopolitics got worse and the physical flows got better, which is an uncomfortable combination for anyone long the oil risk premium. Two very large crude carriers, the Bahri-operated Sidr and Sinokor's Senegal Prosperity, were struck by projectiles late Monday off Oman near Khasab, each having loaded two million barrels of Saudi crude at Juaymah the week before; no one claimed responsibility and all crew are safe. The US said it had targeted Iranian rocket launchers preparing to lay mines in the Strait, Iran retaliated against the UAE and Jordan, and overnight the US struck Kuhestak in southern Iran with explosions reported across the south. Trump warned Iran will be hit harder if it retaliates further. And yet Energy Secretary Chris Wright said over 17 million barrels a day moved through the Strait on Tuesday, the highest level since the conflict began. WTI is 90.903 and up 0.76% today on a 4.45 million barrel EIA crude draw against a 1.1 million expectation, Brent 95.699, EU gas 73.59 and up 27.99% on the month, UK gas 181.45 and up 28.67%. The haven complex partially came back to life: gold rose 0.92% to 4,368.33 and silver 1.39% to 64.956, reversing part of a week that is still minus 4.89% and minus 4.59%. But the franc did not participate - USD/CHF is 0.81307 and UP 0.18% on a day when the dollar itself was soft, which is the sixth consecutive failed haven test and now a discriminating one, because the market chose the yen and gold and left the franc behind. CHF nonetheless stays at 0 rather than being cut, because the morning file pre-committed to letting tomorrow's CPI at 06:30Z decide it and cutting a score on price action alone the day before the deciding print is the mistake this process is designed to avoid. The consensus is 0.5% against 0.4% now, with TE forecasting 0.6%. NZD also stays at 0 for the same discipline reason: it was already downgraded this morning on the RBNZ track, and NZD/USD at 0.58459, down 0.78% today and 1.66% on the week, is follow-through confirming that call rather than new information justifying a second cut in one session. EUR holds +2 with the ECB hike to a 2.50% deposit rate now fully priced for September 10 - TE's own calendar carries the consensus at 2.50% from 2.25% - though EUR/USD at 1.15881 is still down 0.53% on the week, which tells you the hike is in the price. AUD holds +2 on yesterday's GDP beat and 57% September pricing, with AUD/USD at 0.71684 and up 0.33%, the best-performing major on the week's monthly measure at plus 2.41%. GBP holds 0 with no new UK data and is now the funding leg against three +2 currencies rather than a view in its own right. The practical consequence of all this is that the cleanest trades on the board have rotated out of the dollar block and into the loonie block: USD/CAD, GBP/CAD and NZD/CAD are the two-notch shorts, EUR/NZD and AUD/NZD the two-notch longs, and CAD/CHF a two-notch long with an explicit CPI caveat attached to tomorrow morning.

JPY.when: Sept 18, 03:00Z - Ueda today said a hike is on the table at EVERY meeting including this one, and named upside price risks
JPY.note: Policy rate re-verified on TE at 1.00%, the highest since September 1995, held Jul 31 in an 8-1 vote with Takata dissenting for 1.25%. JPY is UPGRADED from 0 to +1 and the reason is the Governor himself. Ueda said the Bank will consider a rate hike at every policy meeting including September 17-18, that he will decide policy with upside price risks in mind, and he named the three factors under scrutiny: the Middle East conflict, robust AI-related demand, and the inflation boost from a weak yen. He separately framed the 10-year JGB reaching 3.00% - the first time since 1996 - as largely a global phenomenon rather than a domestic policy signal while pledging vigilance. This came hours after Takata, the lone July dissenter and the board's most hawkish member, renewed his push for consecutive hikes in a Sapporo speech, making him the third board voice before the meeting. The market moved on it properly rather than fading it: USD/JPY broke DOWN 0.84% to 158.839, off the 160 line both capitals defended after the July 31 joint intervention, and the Nikkei fell 2.60% to 64,495 with SoftBank down 6.4% and Tokyo Electron 3.4% - equities pricing the same tightening. HONEST CAVEAT: this is a policy-expectations upgrade, not an economic one. The energy shock is a direct terms-of-trade hit on an economy that imports nearly all its oil - the trade balance is MINUS 634 billion yen, the current account swung to MINUS 923 billion, and July household spending prints Friday at 02:30Z. Average cash earnings on Sept 8 and final Q2 GDP the same day are the data that either confirm or break the wage-price case Ueda needs.

geopolitics: The Strait got materially more dangerous today and materially more open at the same time, and holding both facts is the whole trade. Two very large crude carriers were struck by projectiles late Monday off Khasab, Oman - the Bahri-operated Sidr and Sinokor's Senegal Prosperity, each having loaded two million barrels of Saudi crude at Juaymah the previous week. No one claimed responsibility and all crew are safe. The strikes followed a resumption of tit-for-tat action in which the US said it had targeted Iranian rocket launchers preparing to lay mines in the Strait and Iran retaliated against the UAE and Jordan. Overnight the US struck Kuhestak in southern Iran with explosions reported across the south, and Trump warned Iran will be hit harder if it retaliates further. Against all of that, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said over 17 million barrels a day transited the Strait on Tuesday - the HIGHEST level since the conflict began. That is the single most important nuance in this file: the risk premium is in the price, but the physical disruption, so far, is not. WTI is 90.903 and up 0.76% today and 10.60% on the week, helped by an EIA crude draw of 4.45 million barrels against a 1.1 million expectation; Brent is 95.699; heating oil is +13.15% on the week and +121% YTD; EU gas is 73.59 and +27.99% on the month with German gas +25.33% and UK gas 181.45 and +28.67%. The FX transmission changed shape today and this is the thing to carry forward. For a week the energy shock was a one-way dollar trade - crude up forces the Fed, everything else is collateral. This afternoon two other central banks claimed the same shock for themselves. The Bank of Canada's statement says the conflict is keeping energy prices higher for longer, that this has increased upside risks to inflation, and that there has been little progress reopening the Strait, with Macklem adding that more than one hike is available if inflation stays too high. Governor Ueda named the Middle East conflict first among the upside price risks he will weigh at the September 17-18 BoJ meeting. So the shock is now a global tightening impulse rather than a dollar-differentiating one, which is precisely why the dollar was downgraded today while Canada and Japan were upgraded. The rest of the transmission is unchanged: terms-of-trade windfall for CAD, imported inflation for EUR and GBP through gas into the October Ofgem cap, a straight import-price drag on JPY that partly offsets its policy upgrade, an equity headwind for GER40, and - conspicuously - nothing for CHF, which was passed over today even as gold, silver and the yen all took a haven bid. The asymmetry to respect is that a negotiated de-escalation is the single largest reversal risk on this board and would unwind the USOIL, CAD, GER40 and partly the JPY legs simultaneously.
